title: Fit new brake pads into a rear caliper with an integral parking-brake piston
instruction: Fit the two new pads into this caliper.
context: Fitting rear brake pads is everyday work for automotive service technicians and mechanics (about 700,000 in the US). On rear calipers with an integral parking brake the piston sits on a self-locking screw adjuster: it cannot be pushed back, only screwed back with a two-pin tool pressed hard into its face slots while turning, and the new, thicker pads do not fit until it is.
setup: Positions from the robot's view: 'in front' is the distance ahead of the line through the two arm bases, 'right' is from the midline between them, heights are above the table top. Caliper (fixed, cast iron, on a steel bench stand 10 mm tall): a rear floating caliper and its carrier, off the car, bolted piston-up with the bore's axis 28.0 cm in front and 6.0 cm right. Bore 42 mm, round housing 67 mm across, top 61 mm up. Piston: chrome, 40 mm across, 34 mm long, face 68 mm up (5 mm above the inner pad's ledges); in its face a channel 9 mm wide and 4 mm deep runs left-right with a 20 mm boss in its middle, leaving two face slots at the rim. Two outer fingers 12 mm thick, undersides 106 mm up, each 30.5 mm wide with a 50 mm gap between them over the bore, from the bore's axis to 34 mm beyond it. Carrier abutments at both ends of the pads (54 to 64 mm left and right of the axis), at two levels: ledges with tops 63 mm (inner pad) and 99.5 mm up (outer pad), running from 78 mm toward the robot to 16 mm beyond the axis; stops 10.2 mm beyond the axis; lips 1.5 mm above the ears; side plates 64 to 72 mm out. The bridge has an open window toward the robot, between the side plates, from the stand to the fingers. Pads (loose, 200 g each): steel backing 110 x 45 x 5.5 mm with ears 8 mm long and 20 mm wide at both ends, lining 100 x 40 x 10.5 mm. The inner pad lies backing down on the lower ledges, the outer pad lining down with its ears on the upper ledges; both centred 22.0 cm in front, 6.0 cm right (60 mm toward the robot from seated, their near edges 17.5 mm short of the piston's rim), long sides left-right. Piston tool (loose, 160 g): a steel 40 mm two-pin adapter 8 mm thick (pins 4 mm square, 3.5 mm long, 13 mm either side of centre) on a 12 mm steel extension, and a red plastic octagonal ratcheting handle 32 mm across flats and 90 mm long with a black cap; 163 mm tall. The ratchet drives clockwise seen from above and freewheels anticlockwise. It stands adapter-down, pins front to back, in a holder centred 30.0 cm in front and 21.5 cm right: a black plastic block 58 mm across and 60 mm tall with a 46 mm pocket over a ledge 30 mm up (32 mm hole below). Details with no effect on the task: a parking-brake lever on the housing's far side with its cable and bracket, a slide-pin bolt in a rubber boot on a lug at each end of the carrier, and a capped bleed nipple. Nothing else is on the table.
scoring: Judged at the end of the trial, with both grippers at least 5 mm from the piston and both pads, and the tool (put down or held) at least 5 mm from them. Piston back: its face at or below the inner pad's ledges (63 mm above the table, 5 mm below where it starts). A pad is seated when it rests on its own ledges (within 1 mm in height), is in to within 1.5 mm of its seated place against the abutment stops, is centred within 1.5 mm, is flat and square within 3 degrees, and is still. Score: 0 if the piston is not back. 0.5 with the piston back and no pad seated; 0.75 with one pad seated; 1.0 with both; full score counts once it has held for 1 s. With the piston not back the inner pad cannot pass it, and a seated outer pad alone earns nothing.
reset_notes: 1. With the tool's pins in the piston's slots, wind the piston out (anticlockwise, as the hydraulics would push it) until its face is 68 mm above the table, slots left-right. 2. Slide both pads out along their channels until they are centred 60 mm toward the robot from seated. 3. Stand the tool adapter-down in its holder, pins front to back. Nothing is consumed.
fidelity: True size. Caliper and carrier are one fixed body of boxes, bolted piston-up to a bench stand so a straight-down tool can turn it; no disc (two ledge levels keep its 10 mm gap). The adjuster is a 2 mm/turn helical joint that self-locks: a straight push of up to about 40 N cannot move it, an unpressed turn spins the piston on it, and only turning pressed into the slots winds it back. No hydraulics or boot. Brake lever, slide pins, bleed nipple are visual only. Fixed layout, as the board asks.
